newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jordan says Jewish settlements threaten peace.
newsitem.headline: Jordan says Jewish settlements threaten peace.

text.p: Jordan's prime minister met Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Thursday and said Israel's expansion of Jewish settlements threatened Arab-Israeli peace moves.

"Settlement and expansion of settlements are not good practices and threaten the peace process, and we hope that the efforts will make the peace process return to the right track," Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti told reporters.

He and Arafat spoke at a news conference after meeting in Palestinian-ruled Jericho to discuss peace moves with Israel which are troubled by the building of settlements and slow-moving talks on the future of the West Bank town of Hebron.
Jordan, which along with Egypt is the only Arab state to have a peace treaty with Israel, has joined a chorus of Arab criticism of Netanyahu's right-wing government policies.
Arabs view the settlements as illegal, and Washington, Israel's closest ally, called a defiant visit by Netanyahu to a settlement on Tuesday a "very complicating factor".

"I am still optimistic despite some of the positions and obstacles that don't benefit the peace process," said Kabariti, who delivered a message from Jordan's King Hussein during his 2-1/2 hour visit.

Israeli peace activists say the government, which took office in June, has approved 3,000 new homes for Jews in the West Bank occupied by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war and home to more than a million Palestinians.
Most of the 130,000 Jews who live in settlements among the two million Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza Strip oppose Israel's peace deals with Arafat.

Arafat thanked the king for his "efforts to push the peace process forward in order to reach solutions soon which will express and implement what has been agreed upon between us (the Palestinians) and the Israelis."
For two months PLO and Israeli negotiators have been struggling to come to terms on a long-overdue handover of most of the West Bank town of Hebron to Arafat's Palestinian Authority.
Netanyahu says he wants to change the Hebron accord to boost security for the 400 Jews living and studying in the heart of the city among more than 100,000 Palestinians.

On Thursday Netanyahu, a right-winger who inherited the accord from a left-centre government he ousted in May elections, accused the Palestinians of not being interested in achieving a Hebron breakthrough.

"More and more it's becoming clear to us that even though the gaps are not large, a decision has not been taken on the Palestinian side to end the matter," Netanyahu told Israeli newspaper editors in Tel Aviv.

Under an interim PLO-Israel deal, Israel was to give the PLO self-rule in seven West Bank towns. It handed over six. The Hebron pullout was delayed by a wave of Moslem militant suicide bombings that killed 59 people in Israel in February and March.

The main sticking point has been Israel's insistence on "hot pursuit" -- the right to chase wanted persons in the 80 percent of Hebron to come under PLO-rule. The PLO refuses to make changes in the signed deal.

Israeli media said Israel had softened its hot pursuit demand and would accept a formula for Hebron -- the only West Bank Palestinian town with settlers inside it -- like that for other West Bank towns given self-rule.
Netanyahu said Israel had submitted various ideas in the last two days but to no avail.
